**Takeaway.** For binary labels, annotator bias acts on the logit scale, so averaging more reference annotators leaves a shift away from the latent target that does not shrink with their number. The test of [Part II](#part-2) carries over with a new bound for $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ that accounts for this shift. On semi-synthetic data, certification becomes possible once the reference panel is large enough.

[Part II](#part-2) works with the aggregate score. This part turns to the 27 binary labels and asks the same question for each finding: when is a panel of reference annotators reliable for a model–human comparison?

### The comparison for binary labels

Since the analysis applies to each finding separately, we omit the finding index $h$ and recall the modeling of $Y_r$:

$$
Y_r(x)\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\mu_r(x)),
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}\mu_r(x)=\operatorname{logit}\mu^*(x)+b_r(x),
$$ {#eq-bernoulli-model}

with centered logit bias, i.e., $\mathbb E_r[b_r(x)]=0$.

<!-- As in [I.2](#binary-labels), the model enters the comparison through its binary decision $\widehat Y_A=\mathbf 1\{\widehat\mu_A\geq t\}$ (@eq-binary-decision), with the threshold fixed before evaluation without using the reference annotators.  -->
Because the labels $Y_r$ are generated with noise, no 0-1 label can be regarded as the true label of an item. Therefore, we choose the latent target $\mu^*$ as the ``just'' reference and test the reliability of the probability-valued evaluation reference $\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}$.
The gaps are therefore squared-loss comparisons of two binary outputs against a probability,

$$
\Delta^*
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\widehat Y_A(X)-\mu^*(X))^2-(Y_B(X)-\mu^*(X))^2\big],
$$

and $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ is the same with $\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}$ in place of $\mu^*$. The relation @eq-reference-distortion holds with $\widehat Y_A$ in place of $\widehat\mu_A$, now with

$$
g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat Y_A(X)-Y_B(X))\big].
$$

### Why binary labels need a new bound

<!-- REVISED: g_r now uses the decision. Original text:

The test @eq-general-certificate of [Part II](#part-2) carries over to this model; what must be derived anew is the bound $B_{\mathcal R}$ on $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$. As in [Part II](#part-2), $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ is the average over the reference annotators of

$$
g_r=\mathbb E_X[(\mu_r(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu_B(X))].
$$

-->

As in [Part II](#part-2), write $\widehat\mu_r=\mu_r+\widehat e_r$ with learning error $\widehat e_r$. Since the model now enters the comparison through its decision, the independence assumption of [Part II](#part-2) is stated with $\widehat Y_A$ in place of $\widehat\mu_A$, i.e.,

- **Independence:** $\widehat e_r(X)\perp\big(\widehat Y_A(X)-Y_B(X)\big)$. The error of a surrogate predictor on an item is unrelated to the difference between the model's decision and B's label on that item.

With $\widehat e_{\mathcal R}=K^{-1}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\widehat e_r$ and the centered-error assumption as in [Part II](#challenges-from-sparse-labels), it gives the orthogonality condition

$$
\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat e_{\mathcal R}(X)\,(\widehat Y_A(X)-Y_B(X))\big]=0,
$$ {#eq-bernoulli-orthogonality}

which is derived in the same way as @eq-reference-orthogonality.

As we carry the test of [Part II](#part-2) carries over to this model, what must be derived anew is the bound $B_{\mathcal R}$ on $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$. By @eq-bernoulli-orthogonality, $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ is the average over the reference annotators of

$$
g_r=\mathbb E_X[(\mu_r(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat Y_A(X)-\mu_B(X))].
$$

However, the Gaussian assumption in [Part II](#part-2), that the $g_{\widehat r}$ are IID draws from $N(0,\tau_g^2)$, does not suit here for two reasons. First, because the sigmoid is nonlinear, centered logit bias does not center the probabilities: $\mathbb E_r[\mu_r(x)]$ differs from $\mu^*(x)$ in general, so $\mathbb E_r[g_r]\neq0$. Second, because probabilities lie in $[0,1]$, $g_r$ must be bounded. The bound @eq-gaussian-bound therefore does not carry over, and we need a new bound on $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$.

### Assumptions for binary labels

[We make three further assumptions, on the surrogate predictors $\widehat\mu_r$ and the bias functions $b_r$ of the reference annotators.]{.ab-new}


- **Centered logit error:** $\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{logit}\widehat\mu_r(X)-\operatorname{logit}\mu_r(X)]=0$. Averaged over items, the logit of the surrogate predictor neither overestimates nor underestimates the logit of annotator $r$'s mean score.
- **Gaussian logit offsets:** $C_r:=\mathbb E_X[b_r(X)]$ satisfies $C_r\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}N(0,\tau^2)$. The offset $C_r$ is annotator $r$'s logit bias averaged over items, and $\tau$ measures how much these offsets differ across annotators.
- **Bounded item-dependent variation:** for some $\kappa\geq1$,
  $$
  \mathbb E_r\operatorname{Var}_X(b_r(X))\leq(\kappa-1)\tau^2.
  $$ {#eq-kappa-assumption}
  On average over annotators, the variation of an annotator's bias from item to item is at most $\kappa-1$ times the variance of the offsets.

Unlike in [Part II](#part-2), no distributional assumption is placed on $g_r$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What the last assumption means"}

**Item-dependent variation.** An annotator's bias splits into the offset $C_r$, common to all items, and a part that varies across items, so that

$$
\mathbb E_X\mathbb E_r[b_r(X)^2]=\mathbb E_r\operatorname{Var}_X(b_r(X))+\mathbb E_r[C_r^2].
$$

With the Gaussian assumption on the logit offset, we have $\mathbb E_r[C_r^2]=\tau^2$, so @eq-kappa-assumption can only hold for $\kappa \geq 1.$ For an extreme case, when $\kappa=1$, each annotator's bias is the same on every item. A larger $\kappa$ allows biases that change across items, such as an annotator who is strict on subtle cases and lenient on obvious ones. Unlike $\tau$, $\kappa$ cannot be estimated by calibration, since averaging logit differences over items leaves only $C_r-C_s$; it must be specified in advance.

:::

### Testing reliability for binary labels

#### Calibrating the scale of the logit offsets

The scale $\tau$ in the assumptions is unknown. As in [Part II](#part-2), it can be calibrated without the latent target, now on the logit scale. By @eq-bernoulli-model, the latent logit cancels in the difference between two annotators:

$$
\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{logit}\mu_r(X)-\operatorname{logit}\mu_s(X)]=C_r-C_s.
$$

The calibration uses the surrogate predictors $\widehat\mu_r$ in place of $\mu_r$. By the centered-logit-error assumption, the same identity holds for them,

$$
\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{logit}\widehat\mu_r(X)-\operatorname{logit}\widehat\mu_s(X)]=C_r-C_s,
$$

so averaging the differences of their logits over $D_2$ estimates $C_r-C_s$.

The chi-square inversion of [Part II](#part-2) applied to these averages gives an upper confidence bound $U_\tau$ for $\tau$ with $\Pr(\tau\leq U_\tau)\geq1-\gamma+o(1)$ as $n_2\to\infty$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Computing the upper bound for the scale"}

With annotator 1 as the baseline, let $\bar W_r$ be the average over $D_2$ of $\operatorname{logit}\widehat\mu_r(X_i)-\operatorname{logit}\widehat\mu_1(X_i)$ for $r=2,\ldots,K$, and let $\widehat\Omega$ be the sample covariance of these logit differences. Under the Gaussian assumption on the offsets, $\operatorname{Var}(C_r-C_1)=2\tau^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(C_r-C_1,C_s-C_1)=\tau^2$ for $r\neq s$. With $\bar W=(\bar W_2,\ldots,\bar W_K)^\top$ and a candidate value $t$ of $\tau$, let

$$
\widehat V(t)=t^2\big(I_{K-1}+\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\big)+\widehat\Omega/n_2,
\qquad
Q(t)=\bar W^\top\widehat V(t)^{-1}\bar W,
$$

and, as in @eq-scale-calibration,

$$
U_\tau=\sup\{t\geq0:Q(t)\geq q_{\gamma,K-1}\},
$$

with $U_\tau=0$ when the set is empty.

:::

#### Bounding $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$

Under these assumptions, $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$ can be bounded in terms of $\tau$. Replacing $\tau$ by its upper confidence bound $U_\tau$ gives a bound that can be computed from data:

$$
\begin{aligned}
|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}
&:=\min\Bigg\{1,\;\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\kappa U_\tau^2+\sqrt{\frac{\min\{\kappa U_\tau^2,4\}\,\log(2/\alpha_g)}{8K}}+\frac{\log(2/\alpha_g)}{3K}\Bigg\}\\
&\quad\text{w.p. at least }1-\alpha_g-\gamma+o(1).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bernoulli-bound}

The 1 in the minimum is the trivial bound $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq1$. In the second argument, the first term $\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\kappa U_\tau^2$ bounds the mean $\mathbb E_r[g_r]$ created by the curvature of the sigmoid and does not depend on $K$. The other two terms bound the deviation of $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ from this mean and decrease at the rates $1/\sqrt K$ and $1/K$. More reference annotators therefore lower $B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}$, but only down to the first term.

The factor $\log(2/\alpha_g)$ takes the place of the normal quantile $z_{1-\alpha_g/2}$ in [Part II](#part-2). Without a Gaussian assumption on $g_r$, the average over the $K$ reference annotators must be controlled for every distribution of $g_r$ with the given mean, variance, and range. Bernstein's inequality [@boucheron2013concentration] provides such a guarantee, at the price of the logarithmic factor and the extra $1/K$ term, so the bound is more conservative than in [Part II](#part-2), especially when $K$ is small.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Deriving the bound $B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}$

By Taylor's theorem, $\mu_r(X)-\mu^*(X)=\sigma'(\operatorname{logit}\mu^*(X))\,b_r(X)+\tfrac12\sigma''(\xi)\,b_r(X)^2$ for some $\xi$ between $\operatorname{logit}\mu^*(X)$ and $\operatorname{logit}\mu_r(X)$. The first term has mean zero over annotators by the centered logit bias. Since $\sup_u|\sigma''(u)|=\sqrt3/18$, [$|\widehat Y_A(X)-\mu_B(X)|\leq1$]{.ab-new}<!-- was: $|\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu_B(X)|\leq1$ -->, and

$$
\mathbb E_X\mathbb E_r[b_r(X)^2]=\mathbb E_r\operatorname{Var}_X(b_r(X))+\mathbb E_r[C_r^2]\leq\kappa\tau^2
$$

by @eq-kappa-assumption,

$$
|\mathbb E_r[g_r]|\leq\frac{\sqrt3}{36}\kappa\tau^2.
$$

Since the sigmoid is $1/4$-Lipschitz, $|\mu_r(X)-\mu^*(X)|\leq|b_r(X)|/4$, and Jensen's inequality gives $$\mathrm{Var}_r(g_r)\leq\mathbb E_r[g_r^2]\leq\kappa\tau^2/16.$$ Moreover, $|g_r-g_s|\leq\mathbb E_X|\mu_r(X)-\mu_s(X)|\leq1$ for any two annotators, so $|g_r-\mathbb E_r[g_r]|\leq1$ and $\operatorname{Var}_r(g_r)\leq1/4$. Bernstein's inequality for the average of the $K$ IID terms $g_r$ then gives, with probability at least $1-\alpha_g$,

$$
|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}-\mathbb E_r[g_r]|\leq\sqrt{\frac{\min\{\kappa\tau^2,4\}\,\log(2/\alpha_g)}{8K}}+\frac{\log(2/\alpha_g)}{3K}.
$$

On the event $\tau\leq U_\tau$, which has probability at least $1-\gamma+o(1)$, replacing $\tau$ by $U_\tau$ and using $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq1$ gives @eq-bernoulli-bound by a union bound.

:::

#### Establishing the test

<!-- REVISED. Original sentence: On $D_1$, the estimate $\widehat\Delta$ and its standard error $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)$ are computed as in [Part II](#part-2). The test certifies the evaluation reference for this comparison when -->

::: {.ab-new}

On $D_1$, the gap is estimated from the decisions,

$$
\widehat\Delta
=\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i\in D_1}\Big[\big(\widehat Y_A(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X_i)\big)^2-\big(Y_B(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X_i)\big)^2\Big],
$$

with standard error $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)=s_d/\sqrt{n_1}$, where $s_d$ is the sample standard deviation of the summands.

:::

The test certifies the evaluation reference for this comparison when

$$
\boxed{\quad |\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)>2B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}.\quad}
$$ {#eq-bernoulli-certificate}

The probability of a false certificate is controlled by the three error levels:

$$
\Pr\!\left\{
\text{certificate issued and }
\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}\Delta^*\leq0
\right\}
\leq\alpha_\Delta+\alpha_g+\gamma+o(1).
$$ {#eq-bernoulli-false-certificate}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Proof of the error bound"}

The argument is the same as for @eq-false-certificate in [Part II](#part-2), with @eq-bernoulli-bound as the bound on $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$. If the reference is not reliable, then $|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$. Consider two events:

- the confidence bound for the gap holds, $|\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)\leq|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$, which has probability at least $1-\alpha_\Delta+o(1)$;
- the bound @eq-bernoulli-bound holds, $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}$, which has probability at least $1-\alpha_g-\gamma+o(1)$.

On both events,

$$
|\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)\leq|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}},
$$

so no certificate is issued. A false certificate therefore requires one of the two events to fail, and the union bound gives @eq-bernoulli-false-certificate.

:::

### Semi-synthetic experiment

As in [Part II](#part-2), the real data offer at most four reference annotators per comparison. With so few, the panel terms of $B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}$ dominate: with $\alpha_g=0.05$, the term $\log(2/\alpha_g)/(3K)$ alone is 0.31 at $K=4$, so certification would require a gap above 0.6, far larger than the gaps between the model and B. To see how the test behaves with more reference annotators, we keep the real images of VinDr-CXR and generate the labels of many annotators from the logit model @eq-bernoulli-model, with known $\tau$ and $\kappa$.

#### Experimental setting

We generate the labels from the logit model @eq-bernoulli-model in three steps. Each image $x$ is represented by $z(x)\in\mathbb R^{10}$, the first ten principal components of its VinDr-CXR embedding, standardized over the image pool. For each of 27 synthetic aspects $h$:

1. **Latent target.** We set $\mu_h^*(x)=\sigma\big(a_h+s_h(x)\big)$, where $s_h(x)=v_h^\top z(x)$ for a random unit vector $v_h$, and the intercept $a_h$ is chosen so that half of the labels of aspect $h$ are positive.
2. **Logit bias.** For each annotator $r$, we draw an offset $C_{r,h}\sim N(0,\tau^2)$ with $\tau=0.1$ and a random neural network $f_{r,h}$ of $z(x)$, and set
   $$
   b_{r,h}(x)=C_{r,h}+f_{r,h}(x)-\mathbb E_X f_{r,h}(X).
   $$ {#eq-synthetic-generator}
   Since $C_{r,h}$ does not depend on the image $x$, $b_{r,h}(X)$ and $f_{r,h}(X)$ have the same variance. We scale the network so that $\mathbb E_r[\mathrm{Var}_X(f_{r,h}(X))]\leq\tau^2$, making @eq-kappa-assumption hold with $\kappa=2$.
3. **Labels.** By @eq-bernoulli-model, annotator $r$ marks aspect $h$ on image $x$ with probability $\mu_{r,h}(x)=\sigma\big(a_h+s_h(x)+b_{r,h}(x)\big)$, and we draw the labels as independent Bernoulli variables with these probabilities.

The aspects reuse the names of the VinDr-CXR findings. We generate 34 annotators and train a 27-output BCE predictor for each. [A's predictions enter the comparison as decisions @eq-binary-decision, with the threshold fixed before evaluation without using the reference annotators.]{.ab-new}<!-- TODO: state the threshold value or the validation rule used in the rerun. --> Two annotators serve as A and B, and the reference annotators are drawn from the remaining 32 in sets of $K=16, 24,$ and $32$. For each $K$, the test is run in 120 trials on 1,813 test images.

As in [Part II](#part-2), we split the total error budget $\alpha=\alpha_\Delta+\alpha_g+\gamma$, which bounds the probability of a false certificate by @eq-bernoulli-false-certificate, equally among the three bounds, setting $\alpha_\Delta=\alpha_g=\gamma=\alpha/3$, and run the test at $\alpha=0.05$, 0.10, and 0.20.

<!-- ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Generator details"}

| Component | Setting |
|---|---|
| Feature pool | 5,438 unique real images with 1,376-dimensional embeddings |
| PCA features | 10 coordinates; full-pool standardization with population variance convention (`ddof=0`) |
| Aspect direction | Gaussian vector in 10 dimensions, normalized to unit length |
| Random network | $f_{r,h}(z)=W_{2,rh}\tanh(W_{1,rh}z+b_{1,rh})$ |
| Hidden width | 32 |
| First-layer weights | Independent $N(0,1/10)$ entries; second parameter is variance |
| Hidden biases | Independent $N(0,1)$ entries |
| Output weights | Independent $N(0,0.1^2/32)$ entries |
| Average offsets | Independent $C_{r,h}\sim N(0,0.1^2)$ |
| Item-centering | Subtract the mean of $f_{r,h}$ over the full pool |
| Labels | Conditionally independent Bernoulli draws given the generated probabilities |
| Panel and seed | 34 annotators, 27 aspects, master seed 42 |

::: -->

#### Result

For each aspect, $K$, and $\alpha$, we call the fraction of the 120 trials in which the test certifies the reference the *certification rate*. A certification means that the $K$ reference annotators form a reliable reference for the model–human comparison between $\widehat\mu_A$ and $Y_B$ on that aspect. @fig-synthetic-bernoulli-task2 shows that the certification rate increases with $K$. At $\alpha=0.10$, it is 0% with $K=16$ and 100% with $K=32$ for every aspect, while with $K=24$ it ranges from 0% to 100% across aspects. For example, for Aortic enlargement at $\alpha=0.10$, the certification rate is 0% with $K=16$, 63.3% with $K=24$, and 100% with $K=32$. More reference annotators shrink the two panel terms of $B_{\mathcal R}^{\mathrm{Bern}}$, so smaller gaps between the model and B can be certified.
